analysis.one_liner: Extends federal debt-collection protections to government debts and caps collector fees at 10%.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bring debts people owe to federal agencies — fines, fees, overpayments — under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, the main federal law governing private debt collectors. It would stop agencies from selling or handing a debt to a private collector until 90 days after it goes unpaid, require three written warnings before that happens, cap collection charges at 10% of what is collected, and order a government study of how governments at all levels use private debt collectors.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who owe money to federal agencies — fines, penalties, fees, or benefit overpayments — gain the right to the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act's protections against harassment and abusive tactics, get advance notice before their debt is sold to a private collector, and face collection charges capped at 10% of the amount collected and tied to actual costs [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People owing federal fines, fees, or overpayments

how_it_helps.text: Redefines 'debt' under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to include money owed to federal agencies that is at least 180 days past due, closing a gap that left federal debts largely outside the law's protections [S2] [S3].

Requires a federal agency to wait 90 days after a debt becomes delinquent before selling or transferring it to a private collector, and to notify the consumer three times — at least 30 days apart — before doing so [S2] [S3].

Caps collection charges on federal debts at 10% of the amount collected, requires them to be reasonable in relation to actual collection costs, and requires them to be authorized by the agency's contract with the collector [S2] [S3].

Directs the Government Accountability Office to study how federal, state, and local governments hire private debt collectors, including the fees charged to debtors, revenue-sharing arrangements, and whether collectors enjoy legal immunity or escape the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private debt collection firms that collect debts for federal agencies would bear the cost: their fees would be capped and subject to contract and cost justification, they would face the full set of Fair Debt Collection Practices Act rules on government debts, and agencies would have to wait 90 days and give three notices before referring debts, slowing the flow of new accounts [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill does not eliminate add-on charges — it permits collectors to keep charging up to 10% of the amount collected on top of the underlying debt, as long as the fee is written into their government contract [S3].

The 90-day waiting period and three separate 30-day-spaced notices would delay collection of legitimate government debts, which could increase losses to taxpayers from uncollected fines and overpayments [S3].
Expanding the law's definition of 'debt collector' to cover collectors of 'alleged' federal obligations could expose collection firms to more litigation and compliance costs on disputed debts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real but modest: they cover only debts owed to federal agencies, and even then only after 180 days past due, and they still allow collectors to charge up to 10% surcharges. The costs fall on collection contractors and slightly delay collections. On balance it is a targeted consumer-protection measure with manageable costs, and its call for a government-wide study of collection contracting could have surfaced larger problems at the state and local level.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mia Love introduced the bill on June 9, 2016, joined by Representatives Keith Ellison, Emanuel Cleaver, and French Hill — two Republicans and two Democrats [S3] [S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, its only committee assignment [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection firms that collect debts for federal agencies came out ahead: they avoided the 10% fee cap, the cost-justification requirement, and full application of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to government debts, and kept operating under the existing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors working for federal agencies

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — two Republicans (Love and Hill) and two Democrats (Ellison and Cleaver) put their names on the bill — so its death in committee was not a partisan floor fight but a lack of committee action.

industries.note: The bill would have brought debts owed to federal agencies squarely under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, capped collection charges at 10% of amounts collected, and required a 90-day wait and three consumer notices before agencies hand over debts — all of which cut into fee revenue and add compliance costs. At the same time, it would have formally defined and legitimized the collection of federal debts as these firms' business, so its passage would have regulated the industry while confirming its role in collecting government money from ordinary people.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local governments as creditors
industries.note: Agencies would face new procedures — a 90-day delay, three notices, and contract-based fee limits — before using private collectors, and the GAO study would have examined their contracting practices, fees charged to debtors, and revenue-sharing deals. Governments would lose some collection speed and flexibility but gain a public accounting of how they and their contractors operate.
